newsitem.title: GAMBIA: Army ruler ahead in Gambia presidential poll.
newsitem.headline: Army ruler ahead in Gambia presidential poll.

text.p: Military ruler Yahya Jammeh retook the lead in Gambia's presidential poll on Friday with results from more than half the constituencies officially declared.
Although results declared were from more than half the constituencies in the West African country ballots counted represented less than 40 percent of total.
Returns issued from 28 of 45 constituencies put Jammeh ahead with 76,790 votes and his strongest challenger, lawyer Ousainou Darboe with 58,356.
Constutituencies still to be counted include four of the country's biggest, two of them Darboe strongholds.
"The race is still wide open," a commentator said on state television, which announced the official results live.

Two marginal civilian candidates -- hotel manager Amath Bah of the National Reconciliation Party (NRP) and Sidia Jatta of the small People's Democratic Organisation for Independence and Socialism -- scored 9,905 and 3,125 respectively.

An eventual Jammeh win could stoke discontent among democracy campaigners faced with a new political challenge: coupmakers exploiting the advantage of incumbency to legtimise their rule through the ballot box. Such elections have left political tension in their wake in Niger and Chad.
Jammeh, 31, seized power in a 1994 coup, toppling elected president Sir Dawda Jawara who had ruled the the tiny country of one million people since independence from Britain in 1965.

He resigned from the army last month to face the electorate in elections he offered early following Western pressure after his coup. Western creditors froze aid and some put a temporary ban on their nationals travelling to the tourist haven.
Jammeh turned to Libya, Cuba and Taiwan who gave aid for new projects in health, education and infrastructure he has openly cited to woo voters.

Jammeh and military associates formed the Alliance for Patriotic Reorientation and Construction which nominated him. He banned the main opposition parties and experienced politicians who served under Jawara, now exiled in Britain.

Legal experts say a Jammeh defeat could create greater trouble. Both the constitution and the electoral law are ambiguous as to when Jammeh's AFPRC military ruling council should hand over power in the event of electoral defeat.
"The transition is so awkwardly designed that it leaves complete control in the hands of the AFPRC," a Western diplomat said. "This is a recipe for a particularly unstable situation."
The Commonwealth and the United Nations described the electoral law and constitutional arrangements as flawed and called off plans to send observers for the poll.
But experts from the two organisations are on secondment to the Provisional Independent Electoral Commission, helping with logistics, voter education, legal affairs and media relations.

The officials from Canada, Britain, New Zealand, India and Nigeria, backed by computers, are the backbone of a sleek and relaxed operation delivering some of the fastest and least contentious electoral results seen recently in the region.
